replacements.text: Strongest feature: Craig converts the disciples’ unexpected resurrection belief, contrary to Jewish expectations, into an explanandum, reinforced by transformative conviction and judgments from Johnson and Wright. Principal limitation: Unexpected belief and transformation do not uniquely establish bodily resurrection; Jewish expectations, grief experiences, cognitive reinterpretation, group dynamics, and developing tradition remain inadequately documented or comparatively assessed. Live burden: Craig must substantiate these claims and show resurrection outpredicts natural and social pathways, while Flew must present a historically supported alternative rather than abstract possibility. Locked score: The exact 76 reflects logical coherence 74, evidence warrant 67, responsiveness 89, relevance and burden 82, precision and clarity 81, and calibration and charity 61, rewarding direct relevance while discounting evidential gaps, nonexclusive inference, and inadequate comparison.

Strongest feature: Craig distinguishes evidential insufficiency from explaining the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples’ faith, making Flew’s undeveloped naturalistic account pertinent comparatively. Principal limitation: A skeptic need not supply an alternative when Craig has not secured resurrection’s factual basis or comparative superiority, and this framing bypasses Flew’s delayed-document and Pauline-vision arguments. Live burden: Craig must defend the explananda and show resurrection outpredicts natural mechanisms, while Flew should specify facts granted, how source criticism undermines them, and why no unified alternative is required. Locked score: The exact 70 reflects logical coherence 67, evidence warrant 63, responsiveness 74, relevance and burden 78, precision and clarity 82, and calibration and charity 60, crediting the comparative challenge while penalizing burden shifting, assumed evidence, incomplete engagement, and uncharitable framing.
